artifact.recommendation: Start signing with the new key immediately while temporarily verifying tokens signed by both the old and new keys. Retain the old public verification key for 45 minutes plus a small operational buffer, never exceeding the 24-hour policy limit, then remove it.
reasoning: This immediately stops use of the old private key for signing while preserving validity of already-issued access tokens.
Because access tokens expire after 45 minutes, dual verification for at least that lifetime allows old-key tokens to expire naturally and minimizes forced logouts.
Refresh tokens are validated server-side, so refreshed access tokens can be issued under the new key without requiring client updates.
All services can load two verification keys without restarting, making the transition operationally feasible.
Clients rely on server-published public keys rather than embedded signing keys, so slow client-version adoption does not require postponing rotation.
considerations: Record the exact cutoff time for old-key signing and ensure clock synchronization across issuers and verifiers.
Publish/load the new public key before switching signing, then confirm every verifier recognizes it.
Keep both public keys available during the overlap, monitor signature failures and authentication rates, and remove the old verification key only after the final old-key access token has expired.
Use token issuance timestamps or key identifiers to detect any unexpected old-key signing after cutoff.
A buffer beyond 45 minutes should cover clock skew and propagation delay while remaining well below 24 hours.
assumptions: The 45-minute access-token lifetime is enforced and cannot be extended after issuance.
Refresh-token validation does not depend on the retired signing private key.
Services can receive the new verification key before the signing switch.
No separate token class signed by the old key has a lifetime longer than 45 minutes.
risks: Removing old-key verification too early could reject still-valid access tokens and cause logouts above the 2 percent threshold.
Keeping old-key verification longer than necessary increases exposure if forged old-key tokens exist, although disabling the old private key prevents legitimate new issuance.
Configuration propagation failures could cause some services to reject new-key tokens.
Clock skew or token-lifetime exceptions could make a strict 45-minute cutoff unsafe.
evidence_needed: Inventory of every token type and its maximum effective lifetime.
Confirmation that the old private key is disabled across all signing paths at the cutoff.
Deployment telemetry proving all verification services loaded the new key before signing switched.
Authentication-error and forced-logout metrics during the overlap.
Measured maximum clock skew and key-distribution propagation time to set the operational buffer.

citations.claim: Access tokens expire after 45 minutes and refresh tokens are validated server-side.
All deployed services can load two verification keys without a restart.
Planned verification-key overlap may last no more than 24 hours.
Old-key signing can be disabled while retaining its public verification material.

artifact.recommendation: Start signing with the new key immediately while temporarily verifying tokens signed by either the old or new key. Retain the old public verification key for 45 minutes, then remove it—well within the permitted 24-hour maximum overlap.
reasoning: This immediately stops use of the old private key for signing while preserving validity of already-issued access tokens.
Because access tokens expire after 45 minutes, a 45-minute verification overlap allows all legitimately issued old-key access tokens to age out naturally.
Refresh tokens are validated server-side, so refreshed access tokens can be issued under the new key without requiring client updates.
All deployed services can hold both verification keys without restarting, making the transition operationally feasible.
Clients rely on server-published public keys rather than embedded signing keys, so slow legacy-client updates do not require continued old-key signing.

Immediate replacement with new-key-only verification could invalidate active access tokens and jeopardize the 2 percent forced-logout limit; continued old-key signing violates the requirement that old-key signing stop immediately.
considerations: Publish and load the new public key across every verifier before switching signing to the new private key.
Keep the old key verification-only; disable and securely retire the old private signing capability at the cutover.
Base removal timing on the last possible old-key token issuance, allowing for documented clock skew and propagation delay if those are not already included in the 45-minute lifetime.
Monitor signature failures, refresh failures, authentication rates, and logout rates during and after rotation.
Use explicit key identifiers in token headers and key publication to ensure deterministic key selection.
assumptions: The 45-minute expiration is an enforced maximum access-token lifetime with no exceptional longer-lived access tokens.
Services can distinguish the two keys, such as through a key identifier.
New-key publication and verifier loading can be completed before signing cutover.
Clock skew and deployment propagation are bounded and small enough to fit within the permitted 24-hour overlap.
Disabling old-key signing does not prevent retention of its public verification material.
risks: Removing the old verification key exactly at 45 minutes could reject boundary-case tokens if clocks are skewed or cutover propagation is delayed.
A verifier that fails to load the new public key before cutover will reject newly issued tokens.

If the old private key is suspected compromised, even a verification-only overlap preserves acceptance of malicious old-key tokens until removal; a shorter overlap or emergency revocation may then be necessary despite logout impact.
Incorrect key identifiers or cache behavior could cause verification failures during dual-key operation.
evidence_needed: Measured maximum clock skew and public-key cache/propagation delay to set the precise overlap beyond the nominal 45-minute token lifetime.
Confirmation that no access-token class, offline token, or exceptional session exceeds 45 minutes.
A pre-cutover inventory or readiness check proving every verification service has loaded the new public key.
Clarification whether rotation is planned handling-process replacement or response to suspected key compromise.
Telemetry capable of measuring forced logouts against the 2 percent threshold.

citations.claim: Access tokens expire after 45 minutes, and refresh tokens are validated server-side.
All deployed services can load two verification keys without restarting.
Policy permits up to 24 hours of verification-key overlap during planned rotation.
Old-key signing can be disabled independently while retaining public verification material.
Clients use server-published public keys, so signing-key rotation is not dependent on embedding updated keys in client releases.
The old key must stop signing immediately, while temporary verification remains permissible.

strengths: Both reports select the only option that satisfies the immediate signing cutoff while minimizing disruption: sign with the new key and temporarily verify both keys.
The reasoning correctly connects the 45-minute access-token lifetime and server-side refresh validation to a rotation that does not depend on client upgrades.
The reports appropriately require distributing the new public key to every verifier before switching signing and monitoring authentication failures during the transition.
They identify clock skew, propagation delay, exceptional token lifetimes, and incomplete verifier rollout as material operational concerns.
The recommendations remain within the stated 24-hour maximum overlap and cite the relevant supplied evidence.
weaknesses: Research-2 recommends removal at 45 minutes while simultaneously acknowledging that clock skew and propagation delay may require additional overlap; its headline recommendation is therefore too rigid.
Research-1's phrase "45 minutes plus a small operational buffer" is directionally sound but does not define how the buffer will be measured or approved.
Neither report provides an explicit rollback or containment procedure if some verifiers fail to load the new key after cutover.
Neither report translates the 2 percent forced-logout constraint into a concrete measurement window, denominator, alert threshold, or stop condition.
The legacy-client statistic is not used quantitatively, although evidence e6 makes client age largely irrelevant to signing-key rotation.
unsupported: The claim that disabling the old private key prevents legitimate new old-key issuance assumes every signing path is inventoried and controlled; both reports correctly flag this as evidence still needed.
The suggestion to use explicit key identifiers assumes token and verifier support that is not established by the supplied evidence.
The expectation that clock skew and propagation delay are small enough for the allowed overlap is unverified.

Research-2's assertion that exactly 45 minutes allows all legitimate old-key tokens to expire is unsupported unless expiration calculation, clock behavior, and the precise last issuance time are confirmed.
missing: A precise overlap formula based on the last confirmed old-key issuance time, maximum token lifetime, measured clock skew, and key/configuration propagation margin.
A complete inventory of issuers, signing paths, token classes, verification services, caches, and exceptional lifetime policies.
A definition and measurement method for "forced logout," including how the 2 percent requirement is evaluated.
A pre-cutover readiness gate confirming all verifiers accept the new key and all issuers are prepared to stop using the old key atomically.
A post-cutover response plan for unexpected old-key issuance, elevated signature failures, or evidence that the old private key was compromised.
Clarification of whether this is a planned rotation or a compromise response, because continued old-key verification has materially different security implications in the latter case.
incorrect_assumptions: Slow client-version adoption is treated as irrelevant based on server-side verification, but this also assumes clients do not pin, cache, or independently validate issuer key metadata in any unmentioned flow.
Both reports assume the stated 45-minute lifetime covers every artifact accepted under the old signing key; that is explicitly unverified.
Research-2 effectively assumes a strict 45-minute overlap is sufficient despite identifying boundary conditions that can invalidate that assumption.
critical_risks: If the old private key is compromised rather than merely being replaced procedurally, dual verification continues accepting attacker-minted tokens during the overlap.
Switching signing before every verifier has the new public key could cause widespread authentication failures and exceed the 2 percent logout limit.
Removing old-key verification before the final valid old-key token expires could invalidate active sessions.
An undiscovered issuer continuing to sign with the old key would extend the necessary verification window or cause failures after key removal.
A long-lived or exceptional token class could make the proposed overlap unsafe even though ordinary access tokens expire after 45 minutes.
recommended_changes: Choose the dual-verification strategy, but define removal as: last confirmed old-key issuance time plus the maximum enforced old-key token lifetime plus measured clock-skew and propagation margin, capped at 24 hours.
Change Research-2's fixed 45-minute removal recommendation to a measured 45-minute-plus-buffer window.
Add mandatory readiness gates: publish the new key, confirm every verifier accepts a test token, inventory all issuers, and verify old-key signing can be disabled across every path.
Specify telemetry and thresholds for signature failures, refresh failures, active-session loss, and forced logouts, with explicit escalation actions.
State that suspected compromise triggers an emergency risk decision that may favor immediate old-key revocation despite user disruption.
Securely disable and retire the old private key at cutover while retaining only the public verification material for the approved overlap.

strengths: Selects the only option that satisfies both immediate cessation of old-key signing and continuity for already-issued tokens.
Correctly ties the overlap duration to the 45-minute access-token lifetime and keeps it within the 24-hour policy maximum.
Uses the server-side refresh-token design and server-published verification keys to explain why legacy-client adoption does not block rotation.
Identifies operational prerequisites: preload the new public key, verify readiness, monitor authentication failures, and detect old-key signing after cutoff.
Explicitly surfaces clock skew, propagation delay, longer-lived token classes, and possible key compromise as factors affecting the cutoff.
weaknesses: The visible artifact contains two target research reports despite the instruction describing a single report, so the review target is ambiguous.
The reports differ on whether the default overlap is exactly 45 minutes or 45 minutes plus a buffer; exactly 45 minutes is unsafe unless clock and propagation bounds are already included.
Neither report specifies a concrete method for measuring whether forced logout remains below 2 percent or defines the denominator and observation window.
The cutover procedure is described conceptually but lacks explicit rollback or fail-safe criteria if some verifiers reject the new key.
unsupported: The assertion that refreshed access tokens can be issued under the new key is reasonable but requires confirmation that every refresh issuance path uses the newly configured signer.
The claim that disabling the old private key prevents legitimate new issuance assumes every signing path and replica is covered by the disablement.
Suggestions involving explicit key identifiers are operationally sound, but the evidence does not establish that tokens or publication mechanisms currently support them.
The characterization of legacy clients as irrelevant assumes they do not independently cache or directly verify access tokens in an incompatible way beyond what evidence e6 states.
missing: A complete inventory of token classes and their maximum effective lifetimes, including offline, service, exceptional, and clock-skew grace periods.
Measured key-publication and cache-propagation latency across all verifiers.
A precise overlap formula based on the last confirmed old-key issuance time, maximum token lifetime, clock skew, and propagation margin.
A readiness gate proving all verifier instances accept the new key before any issuer starts signing with it.
A defined monitoring and rollback plan tied directly to the 2 percent forced-logout constraint.
Clarification whether the old key is merely being replaced operationally or is suspected compromised, because compromise changes the acceptable overlap tradeoff.
A secure retirement procedure for the old private key, including revocation of access, deletion or destruction where applicable, and audit evidence.
incorrect_assumptions: Treating 45 minutes as automatically sufficient ignores boundary conditions unless expiration semantics, clock skew, and the exact last issuance time are verified.
Assuming all relevant tokens share the stated 45-minute lifetime is not supported by the supplied evidence.
Assuming dual-key loading capability guarantees successful and timely distribution to every verifier conflates capability with deployment readiness.
Assuming the rotation is planned rather than compromise-driven is plausible from context but not conclusively established.
critical_risks: Removing old-key verification too early can reject valid tokens and breach the 2 percent forced-logout limit.
Starting new-key signing before every verifier has loaded the new public key can cause widespread authentication failures.
If the old private key is compromised, retaining verification support permits forged old-key tokens throughout the overlap.
An undiscovered longer-lived token class or stale signing replica could invalidate the proposed cutoff calculation.
Cache behavior, clock skew, or inconsistent cutover timestamps can create intermittent failures that are difficult to diagnose.
recommended_changes: State one unambiguous policy: preload and validate the new verification key everywhere, atomically disable all old-key signing paths, then sign only with the new key while temporarily accepting both.
Calculate removal as the last confirmed old-key issuance time plus the maximum enforced token lifetime plus measured skew and propagation margin, capped at 24 hours.
Require an inventory confirming that no old-key-signed token class survives beyond the calculated overlap.
Add explicit readiness checks, telemetry thresholds, ownership, rollback criteria, and a measurement definition for the 2 percent logout constraint.
Define an emergency-compromise branch that may shorten or eliminate overlap and explicitly accepts the resulting availability impact.
Reconcile the exact-45-minute recommendation with the buffer recommendation; prefer a measured buffer unless evidence proves none is needed.
Clarify which of the two visible research reports is the intended single review target.

attacks: The dual-verification recommendation is not yet proven to satisfy the 2 percent constraint because no definition, denominator, measurement window, baseline, or enforceable threshold for “forced logout” is supplied.

A 45-minute overlap is falsely precise. Token validation may include clock-skew leeway, delayed issuance, cache lag, or exceptional lifetimes, so expiration must be calculated from the last confirmed old-key issuance—not merely the nominal cutover time.
The proposed “45 minutes plus buffer” is also non-decision-ready: an unmeasured buffer can be either too short for continuity or unnecessarily long for security.
Evidence that services can load two keys establishes capability, not that every instance, region, cache, gateway, and verifier has actually loaded the new key before cutover.

Disabling the old key independently does not prove atomic disablement across every issuer, replica, refresh path, batch job, or emergency signing path. One stale signer invalidates the planned removal time.
The recommendation assumes this is routine rotation. If compromise is suspected, accepting the old public key preserves an attacker’s ability to mint accepted tokens throughout the overlap.

Legacy-client age is dismissed too broadly. Server-side verification reduces client coupling, but does not exclude clients that pin issuer metadata, cache discovery documents, or participate in unmentioned token-validation flows.
Server-side refresh validation does not itself prove refreshed access tokens use the new signer or that refresh failures cannot force reauthentication.
Removing old verification support is effectively irreversible for still-valid old-key tokens; the reports provide no containment strategy if failures appear after removal.
A rollback to old-key signing would violate the explicit constraint, so generic rollback language is inadequate. The design needs a forward-only recovery path for failed verifier rollout.

The 24-hour cap may be incompatible with an undiscovered long-lived token class or stale issuer. The recommendation does not state what happens when readiness evidence cannot establish compliance before cutover.

The reports recommend key identifiers without evidence that issuers, tokens, JWKS publication, and all verifiers support consistent `kid` behavior; collisions, missing identifiers, or stale caches could create ambiguous verification.
falsifiers: Discover any old-key-signed token or accepted credential whose maximum effective lifetime, including validation leeway, exceeds the proposed overlap.
Demonstrate that one verifier instance rejects a new-key test token immediately before cutover.
Observe any issuer signing with the old key after the recorded cutoff; this resets the earliest safe removal time and disproves atomic disablement.
Show that an access token issued at the latest possible old-key issuance remains accepted after the proposed removal timestamp because of skew or grace-period semantics.

Establish that the old private key may be compromised or accessible to an adversary; this falsifies the claim that temporary old-key verification is acceptably low risk without an explicit emergency exception.
Find a refresh issuance path that retains the old signer, embeds key-specific assumptions, or forces user reauthentication during signer changes.
Find a legacy or embedded client that pins or caches key metadata incompatibly and fails when the new key becomes active.
Measure forced logout or equivalent active-session loss above 2 percent during a representative canary or staged cutover.
Show that key publication or verifier-cache propagation can exceed the remaining margin before the 24-hour policy cap.
Demonstrate missing, duplicated, or inconsistently interpreted key identifiers that prevent deterministic selection during overlap.
evidence_gaps: Complete inventory of token classes, issuers, refresh paths, service credentials, offline tokens, exceptional policies, validation leeway, and maximum effective lifetimes.
Authoritative determination of whether the rotation is planned process replacement or a response to suspected compromise.
Proof that every signing path can stop using the old private key atomically, plus audit evidence that no old-key issuance occurred after cutoff.
Instance-level readiness evidence that every verifier, region, gateway, cache, and dependent service accepts the new key before signing switches.
Measured worst-case clock skew, key-publication latency, cache lifetime, configuration propagation time, and issuance-drain time.
A precise removal formula: last confirmed old-key issuance time plus maximum effective token lifetime plus measured validation/propagation margin, subject to the 24-hour cap.
Definition of forced logout, affected-user denominator, observation window, telemetry source, alert threshold, and attribution method for enforcing the 2 percent limit.
A forward-only incident procedure for partial verifier rollout, elevated signature failures, stale old-key signing, and failures discovered after old-key verification removal.
Evidence that all refresh-token issuance paths select the new signer and do not depend on the retired key.
Evidence that legacy and embedded clients neither pin incompatible key material nor rely on independent validation flows omitted from e6.
Documented support and uniqueness guarantees for key identifiers across issuers, publication endpoints, caches, and verifiers.
A decision rule for the case where required overlap exceeds 24 hours, including whether cutover is delayed, token lifetimes are reduced beforehand, or availability risk is explicitly accepted.
Canary or simulation results showing both boundary-time tokens and newly signed tokens succeed while session-loss metrics remain below the constraint.
Secure old-private-key retirement controls, including access revocation, destruction or escrow treatment, auditability, and confirmation that backups cannot resume signing.

accepted_criticisms: The overlap cannot be fixed at exactly 45 minutes or an undefined “small buffer”; removal must be calculated from the last confirmed old-key issuance plus the maximum effective token lifetime and measured skew/propagation margin.
The 2 percent forced-logout constraint needs an explicit definition, denominator, observation window, telemetry source, and enforcement threshold.
Dual-key loading capability does not prove deployment readiness; every verifier instance, region, gateway, and cache must be shown to accept a new-key test token before cutover.
Independent disablement capability does not prove every issuer, replica, refresh path, or emergency signer stops old-key signing; issuance must be inventoried and audited.
Server-side refresh validation does not prove every refresh path issues new-key access tokens without forcing reauthentication.
The recommendation needs a forward-only containment procedure because rollback to old-key signing would violate the constraint.
The 24-hour cap requires a decision rule: delay cutover or reduce token lifetimes beforehand if the calculated safe overlap cannot fit within 24 hours.
Key identifiers should not be required without confirming consistent, unique `kid` support across issuers, tokens, publication endpoints, caches, and verifiers.
If compromise is suspected, continued old-key verification preserves acceptance of forged tokens and requires an emergency security-versus-availability decision.
The reports overgeneralized legacy-client irrelevance; evidence e6 reduces client coupling but does not rule out metadata pinning, stale discovery caches, or omitted validation flows.
A complete inventory is required to exclude longer-lived or exceptional old-key-signed credentials.
The plan needs secure retirement controls for the old private key and a response for failures discovered after old-key verification is removed.
rejected_criticisms: The criticism that the dual-verification strategy itself is unsupported is rejected: among the supplied options, it is the only one that both stops old-key signing immediately and preserves already-issued access tokens.

The suggestion that routine rotation was merely assumed is overstated: the context says the handling process is being replaced and policy explicitly describes planned rotation, although a compromise check should still be a readiness gate.

The legacy-client statistic does not need to determine the strategy quantitatively because e6 directly states that services, not clients, perform token verification; it remains useful only for validating exceptional client flows.
A generic ability to roll back to old-key signing is not an acceptable requirement because it conflicts with the explicit immediate-stop constraint; recovery must instead be forward-only.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Choose dual verification: publish the new public key and prove every verifier accepts it; inventory all token, refresh, and signing paths; then atomically stop old-key signing and begin new-key signing while accepting both public keys. Remove old-key verification only at the last confirmed old-key issuance time plus the maximum enforced effective lifetime plus measured skew and propagation margin, never beyond 24 hours. Delay cutover or shorten lifetimes beforehand if that bound cannot fit. Enforce a defined forced-logout metric below 2 percent, use forward-only incident containment, and follow an emergency revocation branch if compromise is suspected.
reasons: The core option remains correct on the visible evidence because new-key-only verification risks invalidating active tokens, while continued old-key signing directly violates a constraint.
The original operational timing was insufficiently precise and depended on several explicitly unverified assumptions.
The added readiness gates and removal formula convert the recommendation from a directionally correct strategy into a decision-ready procedure.
Confidence is reduced because token inventory, fleet-wide readiness, atomic signer disablement, refresh behavior, telemetry, and compromise status are not established by the supplied evidence.

accepted_criticisms: The overlap duration cannot be fixed at exactly 45 minutes or an undefined “45 minutes plus buffer”; removal must be calculated from the last confirmed old-key issuance, maximum effective token lifetime, validation leeway, and measured propagation margin.
Dual-key loading capability does not prove that every verifier instance, region, gateway, and cache has loaded and accepted the new key before cutover.
Independent disablement capability does not prove that every issuer, replica, refresh path, batch job, and emergency signing path stops old-key signing at the cutoff.
The 2 percent forced-logout constraint needs a defined denominator, observation window, telemetry source, threshold, and escalation rule.
Server-side refresh validation alone does not prove every refresh issuance path uses the new signer without forcing reauthentication.
The reports lack a forward-only recovery and containment procedure; reverting to old-key signing would violate the stated constraint.
The token and issuer inventory must establish that no accepted old-key credential has an effective lifetime exceeding the permitted overlap.
Key identifiers should not be made a prerequisite without confirming consistent support, uniqueness, publication, and cache behavior.
rejected_criticisms: The suggestion that the rotation may be compromise-driven is not supported by the visible problem, which states that the key is being rotated because its handling process is being replaced and explicitly supplies a planned-rotation overlap policy. A compromise branch is prudent contingency planning, but it does not invalidate the recommendation on the given evidence.

The legacy-client objection is speculative and conflicts with the supplied scope: e6 states that token verification is performed by services using server-published keys rather than by clients embedding signing keys. Unmentioned client-side validation or pinning flows are possible evidence gaps, not grounds to reject the strategy.

The lack of proven `kid` support does not invalidate dual verification because key identifiers were proposed as an operational mechanism, not established as necessary; verifiers can attempt appropriate configured keys or use another deterministic mechanism.

The inability to prove compliance with the 2 percent constraint from the supplied evidence does not favor either alternative: immediate new-key-only verification creates greater session-loss risk, while continued old-key signing directly violates a constraint.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Use dual verification: first publish the new public key and prove every verifier accepts a new-key test token; inventory all token and signing paths; then atomically stop old-key signing and begin new-key signing. Retain only the old public verification material until the last confirmed old-key issuance time plus the maximum enforced effective token lifetime plus measured clock-skew and propagation margin, never beyond 24 hours. Do not cut over if readiness or lifetime evidence cannot fit that bound. Monitor a precisely defined forced-logout metric against the 2 percent limit and use forward-only recovery actions such as completing verifier propagation, pausing affected traffic, or extending verification within the approved cap—never resuming old-key signing.
reasons: Dual verification remains the only listed option that both stops old-key signing immediately and preserves already-issued tokens.
The original strategic choice was correct, but the proposed timing was insufficiently operationalized and Research-2’s exact 45-minute cutoff was unjustifiably rigid.
The visible evidence establishes feasibility, not fleet-wide readiness, atomic signer shutdown, or complete token-lifetime coverage; these must become mandatory gates.
The context supports a planned process rotation, so compromise-specific revocation is not the governing case on the visible evidence.
Confidence is reduced because compliance with the logout constraint and 24-hour cap cannot be demonstrated until the missing measurements and inventories are completed.

artifact.decision: Choose dual verification: stop all old-key signing and begin new-key signing, while temporarily accepting tokens verified by either public key. This is the only listed strategy that can satisfy the immediate signing cutoff while preserving already-issued tokens. Cutover must remain conditional on readiness and lifetime evidence; old-key verification removal must be calculated, not fixed at exactly 45 minutes.
artifact.action: Prepublish the new public key and prove every verifier instance accepts a new-key test token; inventory every issuer, signing path, refresh path, token class, cache, and lifetime exception; define and instrument the 2 percent forced-logout constraint; then atomically disable old-key signing across all paths and start new-key signing. Retain only old public verification material until the last confirmed old-key issuance time plus the maximum effective old-key credential lifetime, validation leeway, and measured propagation margin, without exceeding 24 hours. Delay cutover or reduce lifetimes beforehand if that safe bound cannot fit within the policy cap. Use forward-only containment and never resume old-key signing.
reasons: Immediate new-key-only verification could reject unexpired old-key tokens and threaten the logout constraint.
Continuing old-key signing until legacy clients update directly violates the requirement that old-key signing stop immediately.
Evidence e5 permits separating signing disablement from continued public-key verification, enabling the dual-verification strategy.
Evidence e3 establishes technical dual-key loading capability, while e6 substantially reduces direct dependence on client release cadence.

A strict 45-minute overlap is unsupported because the artifacts provide no measured validation leeway, clock skew, propagation delay, exact last issuance time, or proof that all accepted credentials share the nominal lifetime.
The visible evidence establishes feasibility but does not yet prove fleet-wide readiness, atomic old-signer shutdown, refresh-path behavior, or compliance with the 2 percent threshold.
evidence: Problem constraint: the old key must stop signing immediately, but temporary old-key verification is allowed.
Problem e1: access tokens expire after 45 minutes and refresh tokens are validated server-side.
Problem e3: all deployed services can load two verification keys without restarting.
Problem e4: planned verification-key overlap is permitted for at most 24 hours.
Problem e5: old-key signing can be disabled independently of retaining its public verification material.
Problem e6: services verify client tokens with server-published public keys rather than keys embedded in clients.
Both rebuttals converge on dual verification with mandatory readiness gates and a removal formula based on last issuance, effective lifetime, skew, and propagation margin.
Both reviews identify the fixed 45-minute cutoff, undefined logout metric, incomplete issuer inventory, and unproven verifier rollout as material deficiencies.
rejected_alternatives: Replace the key immediately and verify only the new key: rejects potentially valid old-key tokens and creates avoidable session-loss risk.
Continue signing with the old key until every legacy client updates: violates the explicit immediate-stop constraint and is not justified by e6.

Remove old-key verification exactly 45 minutes after nominal cutover: falsely assumes strict lifetime enforcement, synchronized cutover, no leeway, no stale signer, and no longer-lived credential class.
Use an undefined '45 minutes plus a small buffer': the buffer must be derived from measured timing and validation behavior.
Rollback by resuming old-key signing: conflicts with the immediate-stop constraint; recovery must be forward-only.
minority: Research-2 favors an exact 45-minute overlap, but its own risks and evidence needs acknowledge clock-skew and propagation conditions that can make that timing unsafe.
A more security-aggressive branch may immediately revoke old-key verification if compromise is discovered, knowingly accepting possible availability and logout impact.

The challenge treats routine rotation as an assumption, whereas the stated handling-process replacement and planned-rotation policy make routine rotation the stronger reading; compromise should nevertheless be checked as a gate.

Maximum effective lifetime of every old-key-signed credential, including exceptions and validation leeway.
Measured worst-case clock skew, publication latency, verifier-cache lifetime, and configuration propagation time.

assumptions: The stated cause is a planned handling-process replacement, not a known or suspected compromise.
The listed options are exhaustive for the requested strategic choice.

change_conditions: If compromise or adversarial access to the old private key is established, switch to an emergency revocation decision that may shorten or eliminate overlap despite logout impact.
If any verifier rejects a new-key test token, do not begin new-key signing until readiness is restored.
If any old-key signing occurs after the recorded cutoff, reset the last-issuance timestamp and recalculate safe removal; investigate and disable the stale signer.
If the calculated safe overlap exceeds 24 hours, do not perform the proposed cutover; first shorten applicable lifetimes or obtain an explicit security-versus-availability decision.
If telemetry predicts or observes forced logout above 2 percent, pause affected traffic or use another forward-only containment measure within the permitted overlap.
If all timing bounds, credential lifetimes, and cutoff behavior are proven to make 45 minutes sufficient, an exact 45-minute overlap becomes acceptable.

Measure effective token lifetime, clock skew, validation grace, publication latency, cache duration, and configuration propagation.
Canary a new-key token through every verifier instance and region immediately before cutover.

citation_checks.note: Problem e1 supplies the nominal access-token lifetime but does not establish exact last issuance, effective lifetime including leeway, absence of exceptional credentials, or propagation bounds needed to prove a 45-minute removal timestamp.

artifact.decision: Choose dual verification: stop all old-key signing and begin new-key signing while temporarily accepting tokens verified by either public key, subject to mandatory readiness gates and a measured removal deadline.
artifact.action: Prepublish the new public key; verify every verifier instance accepts a new-key test token; inventory every issuer, signing path, refresh path, token class, cache, and lifetime exception; then atomically disable old-key signing and activate new-key signing. Remove old-key verification at the last confirmed old-key issuance time plus the maximum effective token lifetime, validation leeway, and measured propagation margin, without exceeding 24 hours. Delay cutover or shorten lifetimes beforehand if this cannot be demonstrated. Monitor a precisely defined forced-logout metric against the 2 percent limit and use forward-only containment rather than resuming old-key signing.
reasons: Dual verification is the only listed option that directly satisfies the immediate stop-signing constraint while preserving already-issued tokens.
Immediate new-key-only verification could reject valid old-key tokens and threaten the 2 percent logout limit.
Continuing old-key signing until legacy clients update directly violates an explicit constraint and is unnecessary for the described server-side verification model.
The supplied evidence establishes feasibility but not operational readiness, a safe fixed overlap, or measured compliance with the logout constraint.
A fixed 45-minute cutoff is unsupported because effective validity may include boundary issuance, clock skew, validation leeway, caches, or exceptional token classes.
evidence: Problem e1 states that access tokens expire after 45 minutes and refresh tokens are validated server-side.
Problem e3 states that all deployed services can load two verification keys without restarting.
Problem e4 permits at most 24 hours of verification-key overlap during planned rotation.
Problem e5 states that old-key signing can be disabled independently while retaining its public verification material.
Problem e6 states that token verification is performed by services using server-published public keys rather than embedded client keys.
The constraints explicitly require old-key signing to stop immediately while allowing temporary old-key verification.
rejected_alternatives: Replace the key immediately and verify only the new key: this can invalidate unexpired old-key tokens and lacks evidence of compliance with the logout limit.
Continue signing with the old key until every legacy client updates: this violates the immediate signing-stop constraint, and e6 indicates ordinary verification is service-side.
Use an unconditional 45-minute overlap: the artifacts do not establish that 45 minutes includes issuance boundaries, leeway, skew, propagation, and all credential classes.
Resume old-key signing as rollback: this would violate the explicit immediate-stop constraint.
minority: If compromise of the old private key is suspected, security may require shortening or eliminating the overlap despite availability impact; the visible context instead supports planned process replacement.

Legacy-client incompatibility remains possible through unmentioned metadata pinning or independent validation flows, although e6 makes it an evidence gap rather than a reason to choose continued old-key signing.
Explicit kid-based key selection may be useful but should not be required until consistent support and uniqueness are verified.
unresolved: The definition, denominator, observation window, telemetry source, and enforcement rule for the 2 percent forced-logout constraint are absent.
No complete inventory proves that every old-key credential has a maximum effective lifetime compatible with the 24-hour cap.
Fleet-wide verifier readiness and cache propagation have not been demonstrated.
Atomic disablement across all issuers, replicas, refresh paths, batch jobs, and emergency signers has not been demonstrated.
Refresh paths are not proven to issue new-key access tokens without reauthentication.
Compromise status, measured skew, validation leeway, propagation latency, secure private-key retirement, and post-removal containment remain unverified.
assumptions: The rotation is a planned handling-process replacement, as stated in the context, rather than an incident involving suspected key compromise.
Temporary retention applies only to old public verification material; old private signing capability is disabled at cutover.
Cutover will be delayed unless the readiness, lifetime, telemetry, and 24-hour-cap gates can be satisfied.
No rollback will resume old-key signing.
change_conditions: Choose immediate revocation or a shorter overlap if credible evidence shows the old private key is compromised.
Delay cutover or reduce token lifetimes beforehand if the calculated safe overlap exceeds 24 hours.
Do not cut over if any verifier rejects a new-key test token or any signing path cannot stop using the old key.
Extend verification only within the approved 24-hour cap if observed old-key issuance, skew, or propagation resets the safe-removal deadline.
Escalate or pause affected traffic if the defined forced-logout metric approaches 2 percent.
next_validation: Inventory all token classes, issuers, signing and refresh paths, effective lifetimes, leeway, and exceptions.
Run instance-level new-key acceptance tests across every region, gateway, verifier, and cache.
Measure clock skew, publication latency, cache TTLs, and configuration propagation.
Audit the signing cutoff and continuously detect any old-key issuance afterward.
Define and canary the forced-logout metric using a representative active-user denominator and observation window.
Test boundary-time old-key tokens, new-key tokens, refresh flows, legacy clients, and forward-only containment procedures.
Verify secure retirement and auditability of the old private key and its backups.

citation_checks.note: The cited claim exactly matches problem evidence e1.
Problem e3 confirms dual-key loading without restart, but only as a capability—not completed deployment.
Problem e4 confirms a maximum 24-hour overlap for planned rotation.
Problem e5 confirms independent disabling of signing while retaining public verification material.
Problem e6 confirms service-side verification with server-published keys; broader claims excluding every legacy-client edge case are not established.
The cited factual claim matches e1; e1 alone does not prove that an exact 45-minute overlap is sufficient.
The claim matches e3, subject to the distinction between load capability and fleet readiness.
The claim matches the planned-rotation 24-hour maximum in e4.
The claim matches e5.
The service-side publication claim matches e6; the inference that no client-release dependency exists in any exceptional flow is not fully verified.
The constraints explicitly require immediate cessation of old-key signing and permit temporary old-key verification.

judge_decisions: Choose dual verification: stop all old-key signing and begin new-key signing, while temporarily accepting tokens verified by either public key. This is the only listed strategy that can satisfy the immediate signing cutoff while preserving already-issued tokens. Cutover must remain conditional on readiness and lifetime evidence; old-key verification removal must be calculated, not fixed at exactly 45 minutes.

minority_report: Research-2 favors an exact 45-minute overlap, but its own risks and evidence needs acknowledge clock-skew and propagation conditions that can make that timing unsafe.
A more security-aggressive branch may immediately revoke old-key verification if compromise is discovered, knowingly accepting possible availability and logout impact.

The challenge treats routine rotation as an assumption, whereas the stated handling-process replacement and planned-rotation policy make routine rotation the stronger reading; compromise should nevertheless be checked as a gate.
